title: Toarcian Oceanic Anoxic Event
summary: The Toarcian Oceanic Anoxic Event, about 183 million years ago in the Early Jurassic, was a time of widespread oxygen loss in the oceans. Uranium isotopes suggest anoxic waters covered about 6 to 8% of the global seafloor at its peak. In Yorkshire, organic-rich Jet Rock and Bituminous Shales record it, and carbon dioxide from the Karoo-Ferrar eruptions is linked to it.

uncertainty.note: PNAS (2024) gives ~183 Mya; Deposits Magazine (2019) says one hundred and eighty million years ago. Neither states an error bar or duration. Years are Ma counted back from the present with no 1950 offset.

as_recorded.value: One hundred and eighty million years ago in the Toarcian Stage of the Lower Jurassic Period

where.modern_name: Whitby, North Yorkshire, England (Yorkshire outcrops of the Whitby Mudstone Formation; global event)
where.historical_name: Yorkshire under shallow seas, Early Jurassic; no polities

importance.justification: One of the Mesozoic oceanic anoxic events, tied to massive volcanic CO2 release and widespread marine anoxia.

reviewer_note: Least sure of the age: PNAS says ~183 Mya, Deposits Magazine says 180 million years. The pin is the town of Whitby (Wikidata), standing in for the Yorkshire outcrops the magazine names; the event was global, so uncertainty is 5000 km. The Karoo-Ferrar link is from the magazine only; the PNAS abstract mentions volcanic CO2 but not the province.
